title: Al-'Azim, the Magnificent
tomorrow: on the last day, what does God do with what you hid?

lines: THE BIGGEST WORD, THE SMALLEST POSE.
cards: Phone held high at a concert, trying to fit the whole stage into the frame. It never fits. Some things are only the right size when you stop filming and just stand there.
Now the odd detail, yesterday's question. In every unit of the prayer, Muslims bend forward into ruku', hands on knees, back level, head down.
And in that low, small posture, the words they say are huge: subhana rabbiyal 'azim. Glory to my Lord, the Magnificent. Why the biggest word in the smallest pose?

teach.b: When a verse came down telling the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to glorify the name of his Lord, the Magnificent, the Prophet said: put it in your ruku'. So the phrase in the bow isn't a later habit.
It's a verse, moved into the body. That's the detail to tell a friend tonight. And the puzzle solves itself.
You don't bow to something your own size. The bow is the body saying what the words say: this is bigger than me. That's today's Name.
Al-'Azim, the Magnificent, vaster than all.
It closes Ayat al-Kursi, the Throne Verse, and Pickthall renders it this way: "He is the Sublime, the Tremendous." Tremendous is his word for 'azim. Nothing you could hold up a phone to.
Here's what that does on an ordinary day.
A fight, a grade, a group chat that went wrong: they feel enormous until you put them next to the Magnificent, and then they find their actual size.
Not nothing. Just their size. And that hadith has a second half, about a different posture, saved for another day.

how: Muslims say subhana rabbiyal 'azim, glory to my Lord the Magnificent, in the ruku' of the prayer, repeating it; the Throne Verse (2:255), which ends with al-'Azim, is recited by some after prayers and before sleep.

o: the one who is great at one thing
the one who lives only in the sky

games.q: the bow and its words — tap the pairs.
p: the bow in prayer, hands on knees
glory to my Lord, the Magnificent
what the Prophet said of the verse

s: the words said in ruku' were picked by scholars long after the Prophet
a hadith says that when the verse came, the Prophet said: put it in your ruku'.
Pickthall renders al-'Azim in the Throne Verse as 'the Tremendous'

games.q: a friend watching you pray asks, 'doesn't bowing feel kind of humiliating?' what does the ruku' phrase suggest?
o: yes, a bit, but it's a rule, so you just do it.
you only bow to what's bigger; the words name the Magnificent.
it's mostly a stretch, and the words are just tradition.
games.why: the bow and the words say the same thing: this is bigger than me. a verse, moved into the body.

practice: Step outside, or go to the nearest window, and look up. Find the farthest thing you can see: a cloud's edge, a star, the blinking light of a plane.
Stay with it through the sit, phone down, and let whatever's been looming find its actual size.

wordCard.voice: Al-'Azim. The Magnificent, vaster than all, the Name said bent low in every ruku'.

orig.note: Arabic: the Magnificent, the Tremendous. said in every ruku': subhana rabbiyal 'azim.

carryVoice: Keep this: magnificent, too big for any frame, and everything else back to its real size. That's part one of the Names, complete.

sources.q: He is the Sublime, the Tremendous.

sources.ref: Qur'an 56:74, 56:96 (glorify the name of thy Lord, the Magnificent)
